4.3 — Chase: The Aggro Radius

Patrol is calm. Now the enemy notices you. One distance check turns a guard into a hunter — and normalization makes the hunter fair, because it moves at the same speed from every angle.

Predict First ~10 min

Read the chase half of EnemyController.cs:

[SerializeField] private float chaseDistance = 5.0f;
private Transform playerTransform;

private void Start()
{
    GameObject player = GameObject.FindWithTag("Player");
    if (player != null)
    {
        playerTransform = player.transform;
    }
    ...
}

private void TopDownMove()
{
    if (playerTransform == null) return;

    float dist = Vector3.Distance(transform.position, playerTransform.position);

    if (dist < chaseDistance)
    {
        Vector3 dir = (playerTransform.position - transform.position).normalized;
        transform.Translate(dir * speed * Time.deltaTime);
        ...
    }
}

Predict: you walk circles around the enemy at exactly the radius's edge. Does it lurch diagonally faster than straight — remember the diagonal tinker from 1.5? What did .normalized do about that, and what would the chase feel like without it? (Fix the memory first, then re-answer.)

Socratic

The enemy finds the player ONCE in Start and holds the reference in playerTransform. Why is that safer than calling FindWithTag every frame — and when would the cached transform become a null disaster (hint: scene changes, like the cave door in 5.3)?

Build Lab ~25 min

Step 1 — aim the pursuit vector. The whole hunt is one line of arithmetic: (playerTransform.position - transform.position) is the arrow FROM the enemy TO you. Minus order matters — subtract backwards and the enemy flees. Try it: flip the subtraction, run the game, watch your enemy become a coward. Restore.

Step 2 — normalize, seen. With .normalized: walking toward you from any angle, the enemy covers the same distance per second. Without it (delete the call, keep everything else): the closer it gets, the SHORTER the vector, the slower it closes in — an asymptote of menace. That is why the turret's projectile used normalized in 3.2: constant bullet speed from every firing angle.

Step 3 — two thresholds, one brain. The enemy now has patrolDistance (3) AND chaseDistance (5). Both use the same Distance call in different modes. Which wins when you are inside BOTH — and what does the enemy do in the moment you step from 5.1 to 4.9? Watch the flip: it is a state change with no if for "switch to chase" — the chase IS the if.

Bug Hunt: The broken hunter

  1. Delete the null check in Start and remove the Player from the scene. What crashes — and where exactly (which line, which method)?
  2. Set chaseDistance to 100. Where does "chasing" stop being a behavior and start being teleport-adjacent — and why is 100 really "there is no patrol anymore"?
  3. Set the enemy's speed HIGHER than the player's xSpeed. Can the player escape at all — and what does that do to the game's fairness contract?
  4. Return early: if (playerTransform == null) return;. Why must this run BEFORE the Distance call — what would Unity say otherwise?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Aggro design

  1. Set chaseDistance slightly LARGER than the turret's range and place them together. What combined kill zone did you design, and where is the one safe line?
  2. Give the chase a memory: once you are seen, the enemy keeps chasing even outside the radius until you reach 12 away. What new field does that need — and does the AP exam's word "state" apply to it?
  3. Hard: LOS — should walls stop the chase? What Unity feature would you have to borrow (hint: raycast), and why is that too expensive to run 60×/second?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Write the pursuit: subtraction → normalize → translate, in that order
  • Explain what normalized buys (constant speed) and show the bug without it
  • Explain the cached playerTransform and its null danger
  • Design an aggro radius that reads as fair to the player
